cells.tense: You are growing it now, in the shape it needs, and you know you are.
cells.ask: Show one person what you've grown before you've decided it's finished.
cells.core:
You're growing something and the growing has a shape you chose. Nothing gets forced and nothing gets dropped — care is doing the deciding, not worry. That's rarer than either the care or the deciding alone.

You can say what you're building and why, and the saying doesn't cost you the building. The day holds two things at once and neither is starved. What keeps it steady is that you're not performing your growing for anyone; you're just in it. When someone names what you've made, it lands somewhere true instead of glancing off. Nothing here needs adding. What it costs to keep is the same attention it's already taking — no less, no more.
cells.sheetLine: You grow what you're becoming, and the growing is yours.
cells.verb: tending what you are growing, in form
cells.place: where you become what you already are

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead there's a finished version of this, and you are already living in it.
cells.ask: Leave one thing untended for a day and watch what actually happens.
cells.core:
You're growing a thing that hasn't arrived. Every hour goes into shaping what it might become, and the shaping has taken the place of the growing. Somewhere ahead is the version that's finished and fine, and you're already there, working backward.

It looks like care. It reads as care to the people around you. But you keep bracing for what it needs next instead of letting it need what it needs. The grip you have on this is tighter than the thing itself wants. Nothing you're carrying is on fire. That's the part that's hard to see from up here — the thing you keep saving would survive a day without you.

cells.tense: The care is still in you and your hands are not on anything that grows.
cells.ask: Do one small task you've been meaning to do and let it be small.
cells.core:
The care is still in you. What stopped is the doing. The work of growing a thing got set down, and the setting down got a reason good enough to keep talking about. The thing is still there. You can name what it needs and you haven't moved toward it.

The distance reads as patience from outside. From in here it's quieter than that and less kind. You're not waiting for a sign — you're just not doing the next thing. What's absent isn't strength or time. It's the contact between your hands and something that needs them for one ordinary afternoon.

cells.tense: The growing is happening right now and your account of it says someone else is doing it.
cells.ask: Write down two things you've done for something else's growth and call them yours.
cells.core:
It gets fed, it gets moved into light, it gets what it needs — the growing happens through you most days. Your account of it says the thing is growing itself, or growing because of someone else. When it's going well, you'd say the same sentence about someone else's work and mean it as praise.

The work is real and the credit has drifted off the ledger. You'd call it just keeping things going. That's the part worth catching: you're doing the growing and letting the story assign it elsewhere. Noticing isn't new effort. It's the same hand closing around the same hour, and finally saying yes, this is mine.

attempts.check: In the Too Much cell the record supports only that the person is tending ahead of what exists, not what anyone will say when the thing they are forcing lands; I have kept the cell inside the instant of over-tending. The reader could reasonably object that they are not controlling, only tired, so the ask leans on a small omission rather than on admitting control. The ask stands even if my read is wrong, because leaving one thing alone for a day teaches the person what the tending costs whether or not the read was theirs. The sentence that would have served me more than them is 'you're already enough' — it is gone.

attempts.check: The record supports that this capacity is running in the person's life, but not that they would describe their own care this way, and not what anyone around them notices. A reader could reasonably say they are simply organized, not tending anything in particular, so every ask stays doable — show one thing, leave one thing, do one small thing, write two things — whether or not the read lands. The sentence that would have flattered me more than them is 'you already know how to hold it all' — it is gone.
